utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. We are ready, I believe, for the next witness, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The next witness is Mr. Martin Pnishi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please read aloud the affirmation that is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, there are some questions for you. We start with Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Could you please statement your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Good morning, my name is Martin Pnishi.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When and where were you born, Mr. Pnishi?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: I was born on the 9th of March, 1944, in Ramoc, Gjakove municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And in 1999 where were you living, Mr. Pnishi?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: From 1973 until today I have been living in Meje, in Gjakove municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, did you provide a statement to the Office of the Prosecution in April 2000 in relation to events that you witnessed in your village of Meja in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Before coming to court today, did you have the opportunity to review that statement?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And I understand, sir, that there's a correction you wish to make to that statement that you indicated to one of my colleagues in proofing. I am going to read out the passage that you wish to correct and just ask you to confirm if the correction is right. This is a passage that is on page 3 of the statement, second paragraph, and it is a sentence that currently reads: "Two of them stopped in the courtyard near the porch. They wore masks and green camouflage uniforms." I understand that this should read, the last sentence: "They wore masks and blue camouflage uniforms." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Yes, the uniforms were camouflage.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is using the colour "verdhe" which -- and the witness qualified that it is grass coloured.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. So this should read they wore masks and camouflage uniforms which were grass colour; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Other than for that correction, sir, are you satisfied that the information contained in this statement is true and accurate to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Yes, it is true and correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, I understand you also made an addendum to the statement which is dated March 2002?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you have the chance to read that addendum before you came to court today?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And having reviewed that addendum, are you satisfied that the information contained within that addendum is true and accurate to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, both of these, the statement and the addendum are in the e-court system under the same Exhibit number. This is 65 ter 02236, and I seek to tender that into evidence at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, two will be received as one exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1033, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Pnishi, did you previously testify before this Tribunal in the case of Milutinovic et al.?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Yes, when I came here for the second time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did you have the chance recently to go over the transcript of the testimony in that case with the help of a language assistant?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If you were asked the same questions today that you were asked during your testimony in the Milutinovic case, would you provide the same answers, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: I would give the same answers, yes. I would tell about the things that I saw with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this transcript into evidence. It's 05064, and I ask that that be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, that will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1034, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will now proceed to read the court summary for this witness's evidence. The witness is from the village of Meje, Djakovica municipality. He describes how since the autumn of 1998 VJ tanks had been deployed above Cabrat hill overlooking Meje. The police were also present, and Serb forces occupied the area. On the 22nd of April, 1999, in Meje village, five MUP officers were killed. One of the victims was Milutin Prascevic. Following this incident, many of the witness's neighbours came to his house for shelter. Already by that date, there were villagers who had been expelled from surrounding villages who had come to Meje seeking refuge. Among -- a number of these were sheltering in the house of Mr. Pnishi's brother, also in Meje, which came under fire later that day on the 22nd of April. On the 23rd of April, 1999, the witness and his family left their home in Meje and sought refuge in the neighbouring village of Jahoc. On the morning of 27th April, the witness, his wife, and his son Mark, returned to their home in Meje to feed their livestock. At around 7 a.m. on the 27th of April, large numbers of police, military, and other forces appeared unexpectedly in Meje. The witness went to the second floor of his house from where he saw that many soldiers and police had surrounded the entire area. At about 7.30 that morning, two MUP personnel accompanied by the persons who the witness describes as Russian soldiers arrived to the witness's house and told him to leave his house with his family as they were about to burn it. They had with them a man the witness knew as Kole Duzhmani from the village of Korenica. The witness began making preparations to leave and put his invalid wife in a wheelbarrow. The men received an order on the radio and then took Duzhmani to the neighbouring house which was owned by the witness's brother. The witness then heard gun-shots and saw the house being set on fire. He saw Duzhmani's bullet-ridden body 19 days later. That same morning on the 27th of April the witness saw that Serb forces had set up a check-point near his house. The check-point was manned by VJ soldiers, police officers, and paramilitaries together with armoured vehicles. The witness also saw a large number of civilians heading towards Meje from surrounding villages. At the check-point Kosovar Albanians men were separated from the women and children and some were sent to the school at the entrance of the village on the left side. The witness also saw that the Kosovar Albanians were forced to discard their identification papers. Later that same morning, police, soldiers, and paramilitaries gathered near the school. The witness took his wife to his godfather's house in Jahoc. From there Mr. Pnishi had a view of the Ura e Travas bridge in Jahoc. He saw Serb policemen march seven young men to the bridge; one officer then killed them all with the machine-gun. Shortly after that, fearing that his son may be among the victims, he witness went to the bridge and checked the bodies; did not recognise any of them. On the 2nd of May the witness saw the bodies on the bridge being collected by gypsies using a tractor. In June 1999 after returning to Kosovo, Mr. Pnishi went to the execution site near Shyt Hasanaj meadow in Meje, he explains that he saw the signs of some 74 bodies that had been burnt there. He also saw evidence of a bulldozer having been used in that area. That is the end of the in-court summary, Your Honours. Your Honours, we had initially listed an associated exhibit to be tendered with this witness -- with the Milutinovic transcript, unfortunately the copy of this exhibit - and this is a map that had been marked by the witness in the previous proceedings - the copy that's in e-court is not legible. So I'm going to ask the witness to go again through the markings of the same map just so this can be clarified and his transcript can be understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 00035 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Pnishi, a map is going to appear on the screen before you. I'm going to ask you to make some markings on this map.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And would kindly ask the usher if the usher could assist the witness in making these markings. If we could blow up the area around the town of Djakovica which is around the middle of the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, in your statement you describe events that took place in your village on 27th of April. I would first like to ask you to look at the map and if you could please place an X to indicate approximately where you were living at that time.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: In the village of Meje.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We see two villages marked Meja, one which is closer to Djakovica and the one you have marked which is called call Meja-Orize?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: I live in Meje. Orize is next to Meje as a matter of fact; the road divides the two.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. In your statement you indicate that you saw a huge crowd coming from the village of Guska. Could you indicate to us by drawing an arrow - and this is on page 4, first paragraph on the top - the direction in which you saw that huge crowd of people coming from Guska to where you were -- Guska and Korenica villages.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Would you like me to make a straight arrow or follow the road?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just indicate as best as you can the direction from where you saw them coming and the direction this huge crowd you saw coming from Guska and Korenica villages were heading?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: This is the direction they followed from Guske to Korenica and then to Meje.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you also say that you saw people coming Junik towards Meja, and you say that they were walking on the main road and this convoy -- there were people from 17 villages - this is the same paragraph. Can you draw and arrow to -- we don't see Junik here on this map as we've zoomed in, but can you indicate the general direction from when these people were coming just with a line?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Junik is up here, but I cannot see it on the map. Junik is close to the Albanian border and then they went to Dobrosh, Dallashi, Rypaj, Orize, and Meje here. Right here. So the people from Junik followed this direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just for the clarity of the transcript, the witness has drawn a line from the top left of the map towards the village of Meja starting from the village of Dobros, above the village of Dobros.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Yes, it's Dobrosh.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, when you say that these people in the convoy were from 17 villages, would this have been villages that were on the road that you have just drawn? Is this where you believe that these persons were coming from?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Yes. From Meje, Jahoc, Rypaj-Madanaj, Ramoc, Dallashi, Neci i Eperme, Neci i Ulet, Sheremet, Dobrosh, and Junik up there. Junik and Batusha are up in the map here, but I can't see them. 17 villages altogether.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And just roughly can you tell us approximately how many people were in this convoy, how big was this convoy that you saw coming from the direction of Junik and going down that road that you've drawn on the map. Just estimate, are we talking of hundreds of people or less?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Approximately 1.000. Over 1.000. There were loads of people. In the beginning people came from Korenice and Guske. And about half an hour, an hour later, people from Junik and the other villages came. There were children, elderly people, all kinds of people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you speak in your statement about going to your godfather's son in the village of Jahoc. Could you please draw a circle to indicate where that is.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Jahoc is here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you speak about having witnessed the killing of seven men on a bridge - and you describe this in your statement, we are not going to go over the details - but I would like to know if you are able to mark that location for us on the map, if that is visible on this map, this bridge that you speak about, the Ura e Travas bridge in Jahoc?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: It should be somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just for the sake of the transcript, the witness has made a marking next to the village he has circled as Jahoc. It's a marking right above the village of Meja.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: It is between Jahoc and Meje.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I asked that this marked map be received in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1035, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this stage I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Kravetz. Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Pnishi. My name is Veljko Djurdjic, I'm a member of the Defence team for the accused Vlastimir Djordjevic. Assisted by Ms. Marie O'Leary, also a member of our team. I have a few questions for you. And I would like a few clarifications. I'd like to avoid repetitions because you have already given two written statements and testified before. Let's pick up where you left off with Ms. Kravetz. You were living in Meja village; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How far is Meja village from Meja-Orize?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: From the village of Orize, a bridge divides the two villages. There is a stream that goes under the bridge, it's called the Trava stream.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: From your house to the village of Meja-Orize, what is the distance?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: But I live in Meje. I live at the entrance to the village. And then there's a road and you can go to Jahoc. It's only about 100 metres from my house, bridge is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't ask you about Jahoc. Can you tell me how far is it from Meja to Jahoc, let's say?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: It just -- the stream that divides them, there are houses on both sides of the stream. And on one side of the stream is one village, and on the other side of the stream is the other village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You are telling me this about the distance between Meja and Meja-Orize?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: I'm speaking about Meje and Jahoc.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Where is Meja-Orize?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: There is a road between Meje and Orize, it's the asphalt road that divides the two, the one that goes to Gjakove, and also to Junik in the other direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And where is Jahoc?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Between Jahoc and Meje is a stream which is called Trava stream, so it's just the river between the two, the Trava river.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So there's no distance dividing them, it's practically one and the same place; if there's one bridge dividing these places, it's practically one place, not three different places?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Yes, you would say so. It's the same area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I call up 65 ter 00035.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Where is Meja, Witness? If you find it, put a line under Meja.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Can you see well with your eyeglasses?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: I cannot see without my glasses and these glasses are not very good either, but I'm doing my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Are you short-sighted?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do have a problem. I cannot see very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That's why I'm asking you, because looking at this map on the condition that it's accurate, and we've assumed so far that it's accurate, you keep marking another village, not the one where you live.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Here is Meje. I can see two Mejes here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Correct. And I'm asking you now, you've underlined the second Meja, so I'm asking you between the first Meja and the second one, what is the distance?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: There are two Mejes here, however, there there is only one Meje. Here is Meje-Orize and Jahoc. This one here should be Meje. There are no two Mejes, there are only one, although I can see two here on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, I see the village of Orize quite separately on this village. Does a village called Orize exist?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: That is another Orize outside Gjakove, but it's on the other side, on the side of Bistrazin. It's sort of town settlement. Whereas where I live in that area you have Meje, Orize, and Jahoc.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. Could you tell me whether Meja is located on the main road between Djakovica and Junik?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Yes, it's by that road, the main road, the asphalt road goes through the village of Meje.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What's the distance between your house and the centre of Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Two and a half kilometres to 3 kilometres, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell me what is the distance between Meja and the village of Guska?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: The distance between Meje and Guske horizontally speaking is 3 kilometres. However, if you take the road then it would be 4 kilometres approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, from your house can you see the village of Guska?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you see the village of Korenica?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: If I go to the second or third floor of my house, then I can see Korenice village as well. I can see some of the houses in that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you underline the village of Korenica and the village of Guska on the map, please.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Korenice is written twice on the map, and Guske also. Shall I encircle them?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Two names are encircled. If you can't see which is the right one, you can encircle both of them.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So what is the distance between your house and Korenica?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Two and a half kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me these black lines, are these roads that are marked here on the map?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: This is the main road. Yes, they do show the roads, the black lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that from Djakovica if you want to go to Guska you would take this lower road here on the left to the intersection and then furthermore to the right to Orize-Jahoc and to the left to go to Korenica?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this exhibit into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D230, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pnishi, my learned colleague started with a correction to your statement, but as far as I understood, there was nothing that you actually corrected in your statement; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Having read your statements, Mr. Pnishi, I understood that you were born in the village of Jahoc. Could you tell me who you lived with in the village of Jahoc after you were born?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: I was born in the village of Ramoc, not Jahoc.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I apologise. In the village of Ramoc, who was it that you lived with?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: With the villagers of Ramoc.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you have a father, any uncles, did you live with them? So I'm talking about your family that you lived with.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: We were eight children altogether. We lived with our mother. My father died in 1952, so my mother brought us up.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pnishi, is Sokolj Pnishi a brother of yours?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: No. He is a relative, a distant relative who has the same last name as my family. He is no longer living. He died about 20 or so years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell me, you said that in 1973 you moved to Meja, where did you live before that, before 1973?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Before we moved to Meje, we lived in Nec village. From Ramoc we moved to Nec in 1960, I believe, and we lived in Nec until 1973. In 1973 we moved to Meje.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What did your family do for living?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: At that time, my late brother who died about 25 years ago worked in Gjakove. Another brother also was employed, I was employed too, so we lived from our salaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any land?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Yes, in Nec -- we sold our land in Ramoc in order to buy a piece of land in Nec.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And did you continue to own that land that was in Nec after you moved to Meja?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: No. We sold it to a relative who lived in Ramoc. He bought our land and house in Nec, whereas we moved to Meje.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You had a house in Meja, I can see that you had a brother in Meja. Were these houses on the same plot of land or were you in different places in the village?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: They were on the same plot of land. When we bought that plot of land, we bought it together. We built our houses on that piece of land together.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How big was the land, the surface of the land that you had in Meja? I'm talking about the land surface.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: We have one hectare of land, each of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Your house, how distant is it from the main road?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: My house from the main asphalt road is about 200 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Between your house and the main asphalt road, are there any other houses?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Between my house and the main asphalt road, there are no houses. If you come from the other direction, then there are.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what is that other direction?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Between the Trava bridge and my house there were houses. There was a neighbour of ours who lived there, his name was Dragan. A road separates my house from his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell me what is your educational background, which school have you completed?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: I've completed secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So what was your occupation?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: I was a traffic policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: When did you start working as a traffic policeman?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: From 1st of January, 1969, up until 1983.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And where did you work?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: In Rahovec.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you live in Orahovac while you worked there as a traffic policeman?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: I lived in Rahovec too, but I also travelled because my family was not with me. I commuted to work most of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you retire as a traffic policeman?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Yes, I had an operation and I was no longer able to continue with my work, so I was retired as an invalid.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You did not have any housing resolved in Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: There was a house where I slept when it was late to go home.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you have any traffic related problems while you worked with MUP in Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: No, I never had any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you have a traffic incident in 1974?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Yes, a train accident. I survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you suffer a traffic accident in Djakovica in 1980?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In 1974, were there criminal proceedings at the municipality court in Orahovac because of that train accident and because somebody left the scene?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: It would take a long time to explain this matter, but there was. Most probably there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you convicted for two months of imprisonment with a conditional sentence of one year?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Honestly, I've forgotten. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pnishi, could you tell me, when was Milutin Prascevic killed?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Milutin Prascevic was killed on the 22nd at 1700 hours. I was in the courtyard. I heard the gun-shots in Meje from the centre of the village somewhere; and shortly after, I could see police and army going upwards and some people from the village then told me then five policemen were killed and Prascevic was one of them. This happened on the 22nd of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. How can you be certain that this was on April the 22nd? What is your foundation for this claim?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: I remembered the date and the hour I heard the gun-shots. I'm absolutely certain about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You gave your statement in April of 2000 so this was almost one year, actually exactly one year after the incident, and according to all the data, Prascevic wasn't really killed on the 22nd. So I'm wondering how come that you know the exact date and time. If you only said April, okay; but you are mentioning the exact date and time in your statement.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: It's not only me who knows this, people from that area know it as well. We can never forget that date because they were shooting at our houses. After that, there was a calm period of five days until the 27th. That's why I'm telling you I will never forget that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pnishi, it wasn't five policemen that were killed, it was only three, if I can say "only."

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: I was told that five policemen were killed, and this is how I recorded it in my own mind. Prascevic was amongst these five policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Which road were these policemen on when they were killed?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: On the road that goes to Gjakove, Meje, Junik. They were killed in the village, in the middle of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you, from your house, see the place in which they were killed?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: No. You cannot see that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this place after the intersection when you turn towards Meja, Orize, and Jahoc?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: You have to follow the road going to Junik for another 1 kilometre or 1 and a half kilometre from the intersection.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell me who told you about the identity of those that were killed?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: The villagers who lived in that part of the village. They left their houses, they fled their houses and went towards the lower part of the village. It's the villagers who told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: When did they tell you this?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: The very same day, maybe half an hour later after they arrived where I was, the police were shooting and they had to leave their houses. They came to my house, we sat down in the basement, and that's where they told me. And we also saw the police going from Gjakove to Meje in their vehicles. Lots of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And who told you the identity of the persons killed?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe this question has been asked and answered already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The question has been asked, not specifically answered. It may not be able to be, but please carry on, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I received a partial answer, but he heard from villagers who had arrived that some policemen had been killed. I'm asking about the identity of the policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Who told you which policemen were killed?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Well, I can't give you the exact names and surnames. There were many people who came at the same time, children, women, men; and they told me that five policemen had been killed in Meje. What names could I give you? I didn't note down the names of the people who told me the information. There were about 30 people who came at the same time. I don't remember who of them told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how did they know that policemen had been killed, did they tell you that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: They had seen what had happened because while they were fleeing, they had seen the scene of the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What did they tell you about what they had seen?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: They told me that five policemen had been killed in Meje. I had heard the shots myself. And they also told me that Milutin Prascevic was among them. And all the people who came, men, women, children, said the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So you can't tell us who told you about it. You can just tell us that the incident happened, no details?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: No, I can't give you exact names. I'm sorry. There were many people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You don't know where the car was, which car, who was in the car, how the people in the car were dressed, who attacked the car, from which side?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: No, they didn't tell me anything else. They just told me what I just related to you, and they fled their houses immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And why did they flee?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Because they were shooting at their houses, from the asphalt road towards their houses. They broke the window-panes and they were shooting against all the houses that were along the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: If that is so, Mr. Pnishi, then how did they manage to leave their houses and reach you?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: They left their houses, they came down the village and to my courtyard. They wanted to leave as soon as possible because they wanted to escape from any retaliation. They wanted to be away from the scene of what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there any fire at the policemen from their houses?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: No, none of the villagers of Meje opened fire. Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: We had never had any problems of the sort in Meje. Meje had always been encircled by police and army. We didn't dare, we couldn't even fire a shot. It wasn't possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And who killed the policemen?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: As to who killed them, only God knows. For eight months Orize and Meje had been encircled, Jahoc too. There were police and soldiers all around us. And I don't know who killed them, only God knows.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: How do you know that it was none of the villagers?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: I am a hundred per cent sure that this person who killed them was not from Jahoc or Meje because had they been from Meje, we would have been killed, all of us. No one would have remained alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us now, where did Pnishi Sokolj live?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Sokolj Pnishi from Ramoc went to Nec, but he died about 30 years ago, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes. And his son is Nik Pnishi; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Yes, Nik. Nik Sokolje, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And Nik Sokolje was the KLA commander in Nec, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: To be honest, as far as I know he was not; but maybe he was, I'm not sure. He was young. Nik Sokolje was really young, but maybe he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that on the 14th of August, 1998, Milovan Vuksanovic was attacked and killed?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of this case. You said Milovan Vuksanovic, no, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, a policemen. But never mind, if you don't know, let's move on. Do you know that Nik Pnishi was in prison throughout the war in 1999, a prison in Prizren? He was released after the war and he came back to Nec?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: You said Nik Pnishi, yes, he was in prison after the war, and then he went back to Nec. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In 1998, was there any fighting around where you live?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: In Meje-Orize and Jahoc, there was no fighting whatsoever. There was no fighting in Korenice or Nec either. Only in Dobrosh I think there was fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, I see here in your statement you mentioned Nec, Smolice, and Dobros as places where you said there had been fighting. Who was the fighting between? Who fought?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: The Serb police and army forces with the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And what was the KLA doing?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: The KLA were trying to defend their homes, their villages, their people, as much as they could. On the 30th of April -- no, I'm sorry, the 30th of July, army forces from Gjakove went to that direction. And on the 2nd of August, Nec, Smolice, and Dobrosh fell. The KLA was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was the purpose of the KLA? What was their objective?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: The purpose of the KLA was to defend their own homes and their own people, their own homeland. They tried to do their best. They resisted as much as they could, but then they were destroyed and everything fell in the hands of the Serb army and police from the 2nd of August, 1998, onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you remember what happened with Orahovac sometime on the 18th of July in 1998, or Zociste or Pagarusa?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: I can't remember. These places are far from where I live.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But you were working in Orahovac. Did you hear that the KLA had taken control of Orahovac and Zociste and Pagarusa on the 18th of July? Was that defending the village?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: There were no news on television at that time. The Albanian new had been suspended, so we did not have anywhere to learn these things from.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But did you find out later?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear about these events. It's very far from where I live, I told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And how far is that? How far is it from Orahovac to Meja?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: About 30 kilometres. 28, 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You were living in Meja and working in Orahovac but tell me, in your time were civilians allowed to carry weapons such as rifles, some machine-guns?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: If they had the appropriate licence from the relevant body, they could have hunting rifles or a pistol, that too with a licence. If they did not have a licence, they could not have a gun at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Those people who had these weapons without licence, did you as a policemen arrest such people? Did you start proceedings against them?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Whoever was found in possession of a gun without the proper licence was imprisoned as envisaged by the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And would it be fair to say that concerning automatic and semi-automatic weapons and especially grenades and heavier weapons, these were not allowed to be in the possession of citizens because licences were not issued for them?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Of course not. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And criminal complaints were filed against such people, and criminal proceedings were started against such people. And the procedure was that the police submitted a criminal report to the Prosecutor's Office, the Prosecutor's Office started the prosecution, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right in saying that it was also not allowed to smuggle weapons across the border, and illegal border crossings were also not allowed?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: It wasn't, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While you were a traffic policemen, did you inspect vehicles, passenger cars travelling on the road, let's say, Prizren-Djakovica or Orahovac-Xerxe?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Yes, I used to stop thousands and thousands of cars, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And this was routine work that you performed as a traffic policemen, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were civilians scared of you when you stopped them and searched them?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Of course, I would think so. If somebody feels that he is guilty of something, they would.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did anyone shoot at you while you were carrying out your inspections?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: No, there was no such case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that on the 22nd April these villagers came to you. How long did they stay?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: They stayed all night that night in my house and my brother's house. The next day they went back to their homes, and for four or five days there were no patrols; we didn't see any police or army. Everybody went back to their own homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you stay at home in Meja with your family?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: That day I left and went to Jahoc. I crossed the bridge on Trava and went to another house. I decided not to stay because they shot at our house previously, so that's why I took my family and went to Jahoc.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When was it earlier that your house was shot at?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: That night. That night when those policemen were killed. When the police forces were coming, they were also shooting at the houses, at the windows. For example, my brother was nearly wounded. The bullet went through the window and into the wall very near to where he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So these people fled from the shooting and came to another place where there was shooting and all the time they were there, the shooting went on; is that what you are trying to tell me?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Well, as it became dark, they couldn't leave our houses. They waited until morning, everything was quiet in the morning, and they went back to their own houses while I went to Jahoc.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but when did it become dark?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Well, about 8.30, 9.00 in the evening. Maybe 8.00. I couldn't tell you exactly, it's been ten years.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: 8.30 or 9.00 p.m., is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Well ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what time was it and what day was it when you left your home?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: We left the next day. Everybody else went back to their own homes while my family and myself went to Jahoc in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, who were the people who accompanied you to Jahoc?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Myself, my two sons, my daughter, two daughters-in-law, my wife, my brother with his wife and son, my other brother with his wife and three children. All of us left.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What about your third son, where was he?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: My third son -- before that day he had already gone to Jahoc. We would not stay at the same place all the time. We were separated into five different houses where we stayed during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Which son left earlier and when earlier?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Genc his wife and his children.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about your brother Gjelosh, did he leave on the same day to Jahoc?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: He also had left earlier, but we would come from time to time to feed the animals, the livestock.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You went to Jahoc to feed the animals?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: No, we would go from Jahoc back to our homes to feed the animals.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. What livestock did you keep?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: I had three or four cows, about 30 pigs, about 100 chicken. They all needed to be fed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you go every day from Jahoc to Meja?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: No, I didn't go every day, but we went every other day or every third day to feed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Was the livestock kept in pens?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Yes. They were kept in pens until the 27th of April. On the 27th of April, I opened the gate, and they went wherever they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe it is time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn now and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pnishi, you told us that you have disability retirement due to an operation, a surgery that you had. Could you explain a bit what was the surgery all about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, what is the possible relevance of that question to the matters we have to decide?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't answer that otherwise I would reveal my intention, but if you believe that this is not relevant, then I will skip this question and I will move on. That's all right. I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, when did you leave Ramoc to go towards Meja; what time was it? I'm talking about April the 23rd, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: It's not Ramoc but Jahoc.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're right, I was mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: We are talking about the 27th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: No, I'm talking about April the 23rd. No, no, actually, it was the 27th.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: On the 27th of April at around 6.00 in the morning, I left Jahoc with my wife and went to my village to feed the livestock. I fed the animals, then my son Mark came. He asked me why I returned to the village. I told him that I went there to help. And as of 7.00, the offensive began.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: When did you leave Jahoc? What was the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And what was the time when you arrived at Meja?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: From the house where I was staying in Jahoc, my house is about 100 metres away. As I said, the Trava river divides the two villages, the bridge over Trava river, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: How did you go from Jahoc to your own house?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: On foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You said that you saw that the army surrounded the entire area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 65 ter 00035 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you encircle the area that was at that time surrounded by the army?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: It encompassed Meje, Madanaj, Rypaj, Orize. This area. This area was surrounded by army and police. If you want me, I can encircle these villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And from your house when you arrived to your house at 7.00 a.m., you saw the -- you saw soldiers and policemen throughout this entire area?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Not in the entire area, but I saw their presence in Meje, Orize, and Jahoc. This area was encircled by army and police. I guess they took up their positions at night. And in the morning the firing started.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And you saw thousands of soldiers and members of the police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: When I went up on the second floor, I can see from there the whole area at 2 kilometre distance. I can see the whole area of Meje, Orize, and Jahoc. There were thousands of personnel and different types of military vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me, the soldier, the policeman that was the nearest to you, how far from you was he?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: The nearest to me were those who entered my courtyard, my house, the others were outside the wall. There were others in the streets, on the intersections. Many of them. It was impossible to count them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I'm asking, at the time when you saw the army and the police that encircled this area, the policeman or the soldier that stood the closest to you at the time, how far was he from you? So what was the distance between you and that person?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: They were all around my house, next to the wall. They were also on the streets, in the neighbourhoods. Very near to where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, were they already there at the time when you came to your house?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: From the house of my godfather where I was staying up to the bridge there was no police presence, and there were no police at my gate. When I went inside to feed the animals, I noticed that they started to advance and to fire their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The first time you saw them, how far were they from you? This is my question.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: I was inside my house on the second floor and in my courtyard, whereas they were outside the courtyard next to -- or around the wall. And then they entered my yard. They came in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, we'll come to those policemen or people wearing uniforms that you are just describing in awhile, but now I'm talking about point 5 on page 2 of your statement, or actually in Albanian page 3, paragraph 1; and in Albanian language and on page 2, paragraph 5, in the English version. So you did not mention any policemen and any soldiers in the surrounding area at the time when you came to your house, so you say, I don't know where they came from, probably they took positions overnight. So I'm just wondering, those that fired their arms, how far from you were they when you saw them? If you can remember this. If you can't, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe this question has been asked several times and the witness has given the answer that he is able to give regarding this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Carry on please, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, can you describe that or can you not so we will move on?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: As I already told you, I was in my courtyard, they were behind the wall on the other side, 3 to 4 metres away. I was inside the courtyard; they were outside around the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me when you first saw Duzhmani, Kole where was that? Or could you possibly, first of all, mark your house, first of all, where it currently stands?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mark it on what, Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document that still has not been admitted into evidence, Your Honours. So now we see the area where he saw the police and the army, so I would just like to mark his house on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, if you can't see it, please tell me, I can't see it, and we'll move on. But if you can, please mark the position of your house?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us proceed. It's quite okay. I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You need another map for me to be able to mark my house on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This marked map will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it will be received as Exhibit D231. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, where was Duzhmani, Kole when you first saw him on April the 27th?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: I was in my courtyard, Kole Duzhmani spent that night in Jahoc. On his way back with his bicycle, in order to be able to go to Korenice he had to pass by my house, by that road. He was stopped by the police at the Pashk Markaj's house. The police took him with them from the bridge. And they stopped with him at the gate to my courtyard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your brother Gjelosh, did he also spends the previous night at Racaj?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Not Racaj, Jahoc; that's where he spent the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: At Jahoc, actually. At Jahoc. And what happened with Kole later on?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Kole Markaj that morning was brought before my gate at gunpoint. They asked him whose house is this, he said this is Martin Pnishi's house. They knocked at the door. I went to open the gate. The policeman asked me, Who is inside your house? I replied that my family was there. And then they said, Take your family out; we are going to burn the house. I went straight to my house, collected my wife, placed her in a wheelbarrow, and I asked them, Shall I join the convoy towards Albania? And they said, No, no, you should stay here. The policemen were staying a little bit further. It was the soldiers who did the talking. They said to me, No, your place is here in the well. They told me to jump into the well. I refused. I said to them, No, I'm not going to jump. If you want to kill me, kill me here on the spot. They started to hit me, to kick me. I fell on the ground. They continued to kick me while I was on the ground. And at that time, someone outside behind the wall was speaking on the radio, communicating with these people who were with me. They asked these people whether Gjelosh Kola was present. They said, Yes, Kola is here. And then they said, Destroy him. While I was still on the ground, they took Kole - they mixed up the name of Kole Markaj and Gjelosh Kola. They took Kole to my brother's house where they executed him. In the meantime I what had gone to the second floor of my house, and I was observing from there what was going on. I could see the convoys coming from the direction of Korenice, from Junik, how they were executed, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell me, this radio transmitter that you saw and heard, what did it look like?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: It was a radio transmitter like the ones that were used at the time by the army and the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you use that radio transmitter when you worked as a policeman; is that the kind of transmitter that you used?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me in which language did they talk, those people standing in front of your yard with the ones who were inside your yard? What language did they use?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Those from behind the wall asked if Gjelosh Kola was there. It wasn't Serbian or Croatian. The language they used resembled the Russian language. If they spoke in Serbian or Croatian, I would have been able to understand it because I understand this language very well. It was kind of a mixed language. It wasn't pure Serbian, I would say. That's where from I could tell that they were not members of the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I'm asking which language was used by people standing outside your courtyard when they spoke to those people who were inside your courtyard?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Those who were outside spoke Serbian. I understood what they said very well. However, the two soldiers who were in my courtyard, they didn't speak Serbian. Their reply was in a language that resembled Russian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you, when you spoke to those soldiers who were inside your courtyard, which language did you and them use?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: I addressed them in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And when they addressed you?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: They couldn't speak Serbian very well. They mixed Serbian with Russian. I could tell very well that they were not Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But those people told you to leave your house but not to go towards Albania, and since you were afraid, what was it that you did?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: The Serb policemen were the first ones to speak in Serbian. They told me to remove my family from the house. I placed my wife in the wheelbarrow, I told my son to push the wheelbarrow, and personally I asked them whether I should join the convoy to go to Albania. That's what I wanted to do initially. But in their reply they said, Your place is here in the well. They removed the cover of the well and pointed into the well, said to me that that's where I belonged. And when I refused, they started to kick me. I fell on the ground, and they continued to kick me. This is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So your son and your wife left Meja and went towards Jahoc?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: That happened at 9.00 or 10:00 when we left towards Jahoc. The army and the police gathered at the school, that's where the main point was. As they left towards the school, there was no policemen or soldier near my house, that's where we left. I dragged my wife, placed her in the wheelbarrow, and we proceeded towards the bridge, towards Jahoc.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, a short while ago you said that your son placed your wife in a wheelbarrow to take her away. Where were they at the time when you climbed to the second floor of your house?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: My wife and my son at that time were in front of the entry door or front door. The policemen executed Kole, then set the house on fire. Kole didn't leave, and that's when I was sure that he was killed because I heard gun-shots previously. Then I went to the place where my son and wife were. And after the army and the police withdrew from the area where my house was and went towards the school, we decided to leave and we set off in the direction of Jahoc.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, when you were by the well, where were your son and wife?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Right there watching what they were doing to me. Kole Duzhmani also was there. Two or 3 metres away from where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did your son and wife come up to you when these persons left the yard?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: I got up myself. When they left my courtyard and went to my brother's house, I went on the second floor to see what was going on around the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And what were your wife and son doing all that time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: They were staying there. Sometimes they would come up to where I was to look around as well like me. My wife couldn't, but my son would come and join me where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: How far is your brother's house from your house?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: There is just a wall that's between two houses. They are next door practically.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And what is the distance between the houses?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Ten metres or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: When you left the yard, when you went out, who did you find in the street along with your wife and your son?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: When I left to go to Jahoc, there was nobody on the street. No police, no army, everybody has left and went to the school. There was no one between my house and my godfather's house. No one at the bridge as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And when did the army and the police leave?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: It was about 9.00 when they withdrew from the area and went to the school where the main check-point was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you see that your brother's house was burning?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Of course I did because there was a kind of noise that we heard, like a puffing noise, and then seconds later we could see the flames and the smoke. It was just 10 metres away from where I was staying, how could I not see it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, what time was it when the house was set on fire?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: It was around 8.00, 9.00. Maybe 9.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did your brother's house burn? Did it burn down?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Nothing remained. All the rooms were burned. I think they used incendiary devices to set the rooms on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the house burning when you set out for Jahoc?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: It kept burning throughout the night until the next morning. Everything inside burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Your house was not set on fire, was it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: My house and my other brother's house was not burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You returned to Meja 17 -- that is, 19 days later, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: 19 days later because I couldn't go to my house before that. I didn't dare. There's only 100 metres between the house that I was staying and my own house in Meje, but I didn't dare go.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me the name of that brother whose house was burned down?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Gjelosh Pnishi.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And where was your brother on the 27th of April?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Before and on the 27th of April, he was in Jahoc. He did not stay in his own house at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When Kole was taken to your brother's house, it was empty, wasn't it? I mean, there was no one living there.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: No, it was my brother's wife who had also come to feed her animals. She had come with her son who was 12 years old at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And when did she leave the house?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Together with us. On the 22nd of April this was, and after that we did not return to our houses. We would go every two or three days to feed the animals.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You said she had come to feed the animals. After she had done that, when did she physically leave the house?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: She left the house when the police went inside her house with Kole Markaj or Kole Duzhmani. When the police went at her door, she opened the door. The police put a knife at her son's throat and threatened her and him, but then she fled together with her son and joined the people on the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did she go to Jahoc?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: No, she went on the main road and joined the convoy of people that left towards Albania. She did not come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And what was the next time you saw her?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Two months later, or two and a half months later when they came back from Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Apart from you, your wife, and son, there were no other persons in your house, were there?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: On that morning of the 27th of April, there was just us. Myself, my son and my wife. As I told you earlier, my family were staying in five different places. My brother's -- my brother's children, they were all staying in different places.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you went from your house to Jahoc at a certain point? I forget what time it was.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Yes. It was about half past 9.00 in the morning. Maybe 10:00. Around that time. I took my wife. I was carrying her and my son was walking behind me and we walked towards my godfather's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Apart from the people in your yard, our son and your wife, you did not speak to anyone else that day while you were in Meja?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: There was nobody else to speak to. As I told you, they took Kole Duzhmani, then they left my house and there was nobody else where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: If did you go into your brother's house, the one that was burned down when you returned 19 days later?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: 19 days later, the situation became a little bit calmer, and I decided to go have a look at my brother's house to see whether something could be salvaged. I went with Frano, and we went to each and every room. Everything had been burned. And when we went to the kitchen, we found Kole Duzhmani still lying there. Frano said, Look at the body. We decided to have a look at the body just in case it was my brother, because we didn't know where he was, whether he had gone to Albania or not. But it was not him. It was Kole Markaj or Kole Duzhmani. Then I went back to the house where I was staying, the house had been totally destroyed -- not the walls and the cement, but everything inside had been destroyed. We asked permission from the police to bury Kole Duzhmani, and they gave us that permission. He was from Korenice, but we could not go to Korenice to bury him, so we buried him in Jahoc.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And everything inside your brother's house had burned down. What about your property?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: No, nothing in my house was burned. But it had been looted by gypsies and Ashkalis, and I could see them looting my house from my godfather's house. They took everything of value that they could find, and I didn't dare do anything about it. I couldn't do anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Pnishi, I have no further questions for you. Thank you, Your Honour, I have completed my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djurdjic. Ms. Kravetz, is there any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I have no questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Pnishi, you'll be pleased to know that completes the questioning. The Chamber would like to thank you for coming once again to The Hague and for the assistance you have been able to give to us. We have your statement and the transcript of the evidence you gave when you were here last time as well as what you have said today, and we will consider all of that. You may, of course, now return to your normal activities, and the Court Officer will assist you to go. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness is Mr. Ljubinko Cvetic, and he will be led by Mr. Stamp who, as I understand, is on his way down to the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. While that is happening, could we mention that it will be necessary to make an alteration to our sitting times tomorrow. We will sit from 9.00 until 12.30 with one, the normal break, in the middle of that. So that will be two full one-and-a-half-hour sessions. But we will adjourn at 12.30 and not sit again tomorrow, resuming then on Wednesday at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Cvetic. Good morning, Mr. Cvetic, are you able to hear me now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you please read out the affirmation that is shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp has some questions for you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: LJUBINKO CVETIC

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Cvetic, can we start by you stating your full name and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Ljubinko Cvetic. Born 27 September, 1954.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I understand, Mr. Cvetic, that you were formally a senior member of the MUP Serbia, so could you please just tell us briefly about your career just by telling us the positions that you've held and when, from the beginning of your time in the MUP of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: I've been with the MUP of Serbia from the 1st February, 1989. I was head of the joint Secretariat for Internal Affairs. In 1990, on the 15th of April, I was appointed head of the Secretariat for Internal Affairs Kragujevac. On the 12th August, 1996, I was relieved of that duty. And on the 1st January, 1997, I was appointed, or rather, assigned to be head of SUP Kosovska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Kosovska Mitrovica in Kosova-Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we look at document 65 ter number 01880.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think that's your letter of appointment to the post in Kosovska Mitrovica Secretariat?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Yes, this is the decision to assign me to carry out the duties of the head of SUP Kosovska Mitrovica. It's not exactly an appointment, it's the decision to send me there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who signed that decision?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: This decision was signed by deputy minister, head of sector, Lieutenant-Colonel Stojkovic. Stojicic, sorry, Radovan Stojicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. How long did you remain in Kosovo as chief of Kosovo Mitrovica SUP?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Well, you see, pursuant to that decision, I was sent there as of 1st January, 1997, but in reality I went to Kosovo on the 16th December, 1996. Pursuant to the decision on terminating my duties in Kosovo as of 30th April, 1999, I stopped carrying out those duties under the decision; but in reality, I had stopped carrying out those duties on the 16th of April, 1999, because it was the 16th of April, 1999, where a meeting was held at the MUP staff in Pristina where it was communicated, in view of the fact that I had completed the duties I was assigned to, that any further need for me to continue there did not exist. And another person was appointed to that job. I stayed with the SUP of Kosovska Mitrovica until the 28th of April because from the 16th of April until the 28th of April I was handing over my duties to my successor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you mentioned the decision or the decision to terminate your time there, could we look at 01884.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And before we proceed to that one, could 01880 be received in evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it will be received as Exhibit P1036. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
