utterances.text: And if we could look briefly at 01884. If we could scroll down on both the English and the B/C/S to the end. The end is on page 2 on the English copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is a decision terminating your tenure at SUP Kosovo Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And it's signed by?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: The decision was signed by the assistant minister, chief of department Colonel-General Vlastimir Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you know his signature?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said you were told at a meeting on the 16th of April that you were not required anymore. Who told you that at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: At that meeting, there were chiefs of Secretariats, the minister of the interior, the chief of the department of public security, there was the president of the interim council of Kosovo and Metohija, and president of the communist party department, late Mr. Zivkovic, and I was told this by head of the department of public security General Djordjevic. He said that there were certain changes in human resources in different Secretariats in the area of Kosova-Metohija, and he mentioned the changes in Kosovska Mitrovica SUP and in Pristina SUP as well as in Urosevac SUP. He informed us Ljubinko Cvetic will terminate to be the chief of the SUP of Kosovska Mitrovica, the position where he was sent to on the 1st of January, 1997, because he completed his tasks and therefore there was no need for his further engagement. The chief of Kosovska Mitrovica SUP was going to be the previous chief of Vucitrn OUP, Mr. Janicijevic. And the previous chief of the Pristina SUP also was terminated at that position, and at that position of the Pristina SUP head was going to be carried out by Mr. Bogoljub Janicijevic who was previously head of Urosevac SUP. At the same time, the new head of Urosevac SUP was going to be Mr. Bozidar Vilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Bozidar Ilic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All this was conveyed to us by the head of public security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we look, briefly, Mr. Cvetic, at the structure of the MUP, the public security section of the MUP. Which position -- well, you've already said that the head of the public security sector was assistant minister Djordjevic. What bodies or organs fell under him or were subordinated to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And as you speak, could we bring up P357 the Rules of Internal Organisation of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm asking you, Mr. Cvetic, what organs or bodies were subordinate to Mr. Djordjevic as head of the public service department of the MUP, or public security department of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we move to Article 2 of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Djordjevic -- actually, the public security department of the MUP of Serbia within its composition had the following organisational units: At the seat of the ministry there was the police administration; secondly, the criminal police administration; thirdly, traffic police administration; fourthly, operational duty centre; fifth, the administration for communications and encryptions; then the administration for analysis and administration for IT or computers. So this was at the ministry's headquarters. All the Secretariats of the interior in the territory of the Republic of Serbia - and there were 33 such Secretariats in total - were linked to the public security department. The head of that department was Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. If we could just look at the rules quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's move to Article 13. It's at page 9 of the English, and it's page 9 to 10 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think this is difficult to read. I'll see if I can find a hard copy for you. Do you remember that Article 13 lists the organisational units that were at the seat of the ministry in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Yes, and I listed them. Maybe I didn't list all of them, but those were the ones I could remember. But in these rules in Article 11, it says as follows: "At the seat of the ministry there shall be the following organisational units: Crime police administration, police administration, traffic police administration, operation centre, border police administration, fire prevention police administration, analysis administration, information technology administration, communications administration, administration for joint affairs of the ministry, and board and lodging administration." These are the organisational units at the level of the ministry, but not all of them belonged to the public security sector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that once again we have a problem with these rules. As the witness just read from the hard copy, he read that this was Article 11. I apologise, Mr. Witness, is that correct? You read Article 11? Yes, well that particular Rules of Interior Organisation is not valid. Mr. Stamp when he read said Article 13 and this indeed were the rules that were in effect at the time. So this is supposed to be Article 13. And if he sees this as Article 11, then this is not the correct rules. And the correct rules has been admitted into evidence as Exhibit P357.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, the document is on the screen in both languages, it is Article 13. So you are correct. You may have heard a translation or there may have been a misspeaking of Article 11 for 13, but the document which is the exhibit is Article 13. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. However, the hard copy that was given to the witness is a wrong document and this is why he read this out from a wrong document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Cvetic, the article which you read that lists the organisational unit, which article is it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: I apologise, I was mistaken. I apologise to the Defence counsel. This was not Article 11, but rather Article 13. So I apologise for this. This hard copy is also very difficult to read. But there was no other error. Even without these rules, I stated which were the organisational units at the level of the ministry's headquarters which belong to the public security sector. And there is nothing different there. So the organisational units which I listed without having the rules in front of me are the organisational units which belonged to the public security sector. Maybe I skipped some of them. For example, I have skipped fire prevention police administration and border police administration. However, the administration for joints affairs of the ministry and board and lodging administration did not belong to the public security sector. These were some joint services that were used by the entire MUP as far as I knew at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Just look at item 2, the police administration. Who was head of that administration, do you know?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Head of the police administration was General Obrad Stevanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I heard the witness say something, but I did not hear an interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Yes, I wanted to say that Mr. Obrad Stevanovic was at the same time an assistant minister. And at the position of the head of the police administration, people were replaced. And for a certain period, Mr. Stevanovic held this position.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In 1999 and 1998 did he hold that position?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: In 1998, yes. In 1999, I believe he was replaced. Somebody else was the head of that administration, but I'm not entirely sure who that was. Mr. Obrad Stevanovic, however, was an assistant minister. And in 1998, he indeed was head of the police administration. At the same time, he was also commander of all the Special Police units, so-called PJPs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Apart from the organisational units at the seat of the ministry, there were other organisational units of which you headed one, the Secretariats of Interior; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could move to Article 2 of this document. I think it's on page 4 in the English version, and -- I am sorry, I'm not sure of the page in the B/C/S version. It would be then page 3, the previous page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Article 2 of the rules which I think speaks for itself, this article, sets out the functions of the Secretariats of the Interior. And Article 3 lists the 33 Secretariats of the Interior that were set up for administrative purposes in Serbia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could scroll in English to page 4, now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct. But Article 2 where it talks about tasks following within the purview of the Ministry of the Interior, these are the tasks taken over from the Law on Internal Affairs, so these are the tasks that are stipulated in the Law on Internal Affairs. And Article 3 indeed mentions the organisational units within the territory of the Republic of Serbia. Within the territory of the Republic of Serbia, there were 33 Secretariats, each of them encompassing the territory of certain municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And how many in Serbia? Sorry, how many in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: In the territory of Kosovo, there were seven Secretariats.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And just as an example using your Secretariat Kosovska Mitrovica, can you describe its territorial jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: The Secretariat in Kosovska Mitrovica was established to cover the territory of the district of Kosovska Mitrovica and it covered the following municipality: Leposavic, Zvecan, Zubin Potok, Vucitrn, Srbica, and Kosovska Mitrovica where its seat also was. But at Leposavic, Srbica, and Vucitrn, there were departments of the interior. And at Zvecan and Zubin Potok, there were police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The departments of interior that you mentioned and the police station that were subordinate to each SUP, they are, I take it, listed in Article 4 of these rules; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Please allow me to have a look at Article 4. Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We see, for example, your SUP Kosovo Mitrovica is at item 11 of Article 4?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we bring up document 02555.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is an organogram of the structure of the MUP. I'm sorry, it's in English, so I may have to explain one or two aspects of it to you. But I think you can understand most of the departments referred to here by the acronyms used. At the top we have the minister and subordinate to him would be the state security department headed by Rade Markovic and the public security department headed by Vlastimir Djordjevic. Now, to the right of that there is a box with police administration headed by Obrad Stevanovic. Can you tell us if that is correct having regard to your earlier answers and to the rules which indicate that the police administration was one of the organisational units of the public security department? Is that correct there or should it be subordinate to the public security department?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: From this diagram which I can see on the screen, I can conclude as follows: That the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia was organised in two branches. The first one being the state security sector or department and the second one the public security sector. Within the state security sector, here we have an organisational unit which belonged to that sector; and within the public security sector, we can see the organisational units, and these are special anti-terrorist units, operational sweep groups, and Special Police units. And all the Secretariats, seven of them, in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. In parallel to this, the public security -- in parallel to the public security sector, there is also the police administration. The police administration cannot be placed at the same level as the public security sector because it falls within the remit of the public security sector and it is actually one of the organisational elements of the public security sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. We also see a line here from the Secretariats of the Interior going to the MUP staff. Were the Secretariats of the Interior subordinate to the MUP staff, and if -- can you also explain the relationship of subordination with the public security department seat or headquarters in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: You see, the Secretariats for the Interior are organisational units of the Ministry of the Interior; and the MUP staff in Pristina, this is a mid-command between the Ministry of the Interior and the Secretariats for the Interior in Kosovo and Metohija. So this MUP staff was established simply for the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, and it functions as an intermediary command between the Ministry and the Secretariats. So the Secretariats reported at the same time to the Ministry of the Interior in Belgrade and to the MUP staff in Pristina. And they received information in the same way, in the same way in which they reported about their activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I take it from what you are saying, that the Secretariats of the Interior were subordinate to the MUP staff, it being an intermediate level of command, but they were also subordinate to the public service -- public security department headquarters in Belgrade; is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: All Secretariats were subordinate to the public security sector and the MUP staff in Pristina was also subordinate to the public security sector. The head of the public security sector established the MUP in -- staff in Pristina in the first place by a decision he made. And he also stipulated his responsibilities, tasks, and obligations. Therefore, all the Secretariats in Kosovo and the MUP staff in Pristina were subordinate to the public security sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see in the boxes for the Secretariats of the Interior the names of persons. Are these the persons who -- are these the person who were head of these Secretariats at the time you were there or at least in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And there are some boxes for some special units above that, the JSO, the SAJ, the OPG, and the PJP. Well, as least as far as the JSO and SAJ are concerned. Are the persons there mentioned as far as you understand -- withdrawn. Were the persons there mentioned the heads of those organisations in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: I would appreciate a higher degree of specification of the question. I told you already that the names listed as heads of Secretariat are correct, but I don't see any other persons. Oh, I do. The unit for special operations, yes, that is indeed the person who was at its head, or rather, the commander of the unit for special operations. The special anti-terrorist unit, the person shown in the box was head of the section for special units within the police administration. And each special anti-terrorist unit had its own commander, there were three of them, three such units. As for operational sweep groups, they do not belong with special units. And neither do Special Police units, or specialised police units, PJP. They cannot be considered as Special Police units. As for anti-terrorist units, I said there were three of them. And there was a head of section who coordinated their work and did all the planning. That was the person whose name was seen in the box.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So the head of the special anti-terrorist unit was Zivko Trajkovic and the special operations unit, the JSO, was Milorad Lukovic?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We'll get back to these units, but I think now, Your Honours, it's time for a break. Could we tender this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document shall be admitted as Exhibit P1037. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We must have the second break now. We resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Cvetic, can you briefly describe for us what were the PJPs or Special Police units?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe, Your Honour, that it is the right time to clarify one thing that has to do with the interpretation and translation and that has been going on for years now. It concerns the PJPs, Special Police units. In some trials this was dealt with by using the acronym PJP, the Serbian acronym so the witness understands what it means. In Serbian actually there are two words, "specijalna" which in English would be "special," and "posebna" is a different word, and I believe the English word for that is "separate." And to avoid confusion, especially when we are talking about units for special operations, SAJ, and PJP, I believe we should -- when talking about these specialised police units, PJP, we should either use the acronym PJP or translated as Separate Police units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djurdjic. At this moment the Chamber would not be in a position to know whether one of those is preferable to another, but we all seem to understand PJP. Carry on, please, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you just describe the organisation and the function of the PJP?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Within the framework of the police, it's an organisational unit -- in fact, as organisational units within the public security sector there are regular police forces; there are specialised police units, PJP; and also special anti-terrorist units. Regular police forces are forces within the Secretariat for Internal Affairs, that are used to control the territory to hold up law and order, and protect citizens and property. Whereas PJP are better equipped and better trained than regular police, and these PJP are formed in larger population centres to deal with more complex security problems. To be specific, PJP were established in 1992 or early 1993, and they were called "Posebne Jedenice Milicije," PJM. Later they were renamed into PJP. In Belgrade, there were two detachments of PJP; in Novi Sad, one detachment; in Kragujevac, one detachment; in Uzice, one detachment; and one detachment in Nis. And there was also a Kosovo detachment in based in Pristina. The Kosovo detachment of PJP based in Pristina was there until June 1998. In June 1998, the Kosovo detachment of PJP grew into the 124th Intervention Brigade, whereas special anti-terrorist units are the most elite units of the Ministry of Interior, namely, of its public security sector. And they are intended only for the gravest security problems, that is fighting terrorism.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll get to the special anti-terrorist units, let's if we can, just focus on the PJPs for a moment. Were there PJPs attached to the Secretariats of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness sit closer to the microphones, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, from each Secretariat of the Interior -- let me start again. Each Secretariat of the Interior in the Republic of Serbia, assigned part of its personnel to the PJPs. For instance, to form the detachment in Kragujevac, personnel was given from Kragujevac, from Jagodina, from Zajecar, from Bor, from Pozarevac, and from Smederevo. The same is true of the other detachments of PJPs established in territory of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, the detachment that was established in Pristina and which became the 124th Intervention Brigade, how was that manned?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: That detachment was filled in keeping with the same methodology that applied to the formation of PJPs in other areas of Serbia. From all Secretariats of the Interior in the territory of Kosovo, various Secretariats provided a certain number of personnel depending on size. For example, Kosovska Mitrovica SUP provided some personnel to form this detachment. Some Secretariats provided a platoon, others a company-size unit. All these formed the Kosovo detachment of PJPs, which became in June 1998 a re-organised 124th Intervention Brigade. To conclude, all Secretariats from Kosovo and Metohija provided part of their personnel to the Kosovo detachment of PJPs, depending on the size of the Secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did the Secretariats themselves have PJP units that were attached to the Secretariats themselves?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Organisationally speaking, yes, because the personnel still remained part of the Secretariat. And those people were assigned to those Secretariats in terms of human resources. But these units could not be used by the Secretariats without the approval of the detachment command, and the orders were given by the staff or the ministry and handed down to the command of the detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier that the PJPs had responsibility for more complex tasks. Could you just describe what you mean by that, what sort of tasks were the PJP used for?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: First of all, those were tasks such as dealing with disturbances of law and order on a larger scale, dealing with clashes and fighting terrorism, preventing disorder. Those were mainly the tasks in which PJPs were engaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In 1998 and in 1999 were all the personnel, the PJP personnel in Kosovo attached to SUPs in Kosovo or were they replaced with PJP personnel outside of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Well, in 1998 and 1999 PJPs from all parts of Serbia were engaged in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. All detachments formed within the Republic of Serbia within the framework of the Ministry of Interior were engaged in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija in 1998 and 1999. Those are the detachments that I listed in my previous testimony, two detachments from Belgrade, one from Novi Sad, one from Kragujevac, one from Nis, and the Kosovo detachment which later became the 124th Brigade. Those were A units, A-class units. In addition to the PJPs from these detachments, there were also B-class units. To be specific, in Kosovska Mitrovica there were two PJP detachments, the 35th detachment and the 85th detachment. And that was true of other Secretariats in the territory of Kosovo as well. PJP units from the complement of Secretariats of Internal Affairs in Kosovo and Metohija were part of the Kosovo detachment and later became the 124th Intervention Brigade. They were engaged not only in their own territory, but throughout Kosovo, as were other detachments that came from the Republic of Serbia proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who or which organ had the power or the authority to mobilise the PJP for combat activities?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Well, decisions to engage PJPs were made exclusively on ministry level, and only the minister of the interior was able to take such decisions or a person authorised by the minister. It was usually the chief of the public security sector who would issue an order to mobilise the PJPs, or in other words to order their engagement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And when they were on the ground in manoeuvres or operations, who commanded them in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: You see, we should make a distinction between a person who is able to take the decision to use PJPs and the person who commands the PJPs. Command on the ground over PJPs was within the exclusive authority of the PJP commander. The commander of a PJP unit commands that unit on the ground, but the PJP unit commander has no authority to make the decision to use the PJP unit. He is able to take command and to issue orders only when a decision had been taken by a superior commanding officer to engage that PJP unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What were -- if we could move on, what were the OPGs? And I think I say with trepidation that that's an acronym for Operation Sweep Group?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Yes. Operational sweep groups or operational pursuit groups were established within Secretariats in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. In other Secretariats covered by the Ministry of Interior, there were no operational sweep groups. In early December 1998, a decision was taken at the MUP staff in Pristina that every Secretariat in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija should allocate 10 to 15 men, the best trained and the best equipped ones from the regular complement of the police force or from the PJPs. And these men would undergo additional training in the duration of 10 to 15 days in special training centres outside Kosovo. And these operational sweep groups were within each Secretariat. And each Secretariat had a commander of the Operational Sweep Group. In other words, all these operational sweep groups were headed by the assistant head of MUP staff in Pristina in charge of special operations. To conclude, operational sweep groups were better trained and better equipped than PJPs, but they were not better trained or better equipped than special anti-terrorist units, they were something in between.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did the assistant head of the MUP staff in Pristina who was in charge of special operations who headed these OPGs, what was his name?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: His name was Goran Radosavljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you now mentioned the special anti-terrorist units, could you describe briefly and basically their organisation and their functions?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: As far as I was aware special anti-terrorist units were established in the city of Belgrade, that is the SUP of the city of Belgrade inn the SUP of Novi Sad and the SUP of Pristina. Therefore, there were three special anti-terrorist units. Their mission in Kosovo and Metohija was exclusively to fight terrorism and to participate in anti-terrorist actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And lastly, briefly, the JSO, what were they, and what organisational department did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: The special operations unit was established within the public security sector and belonged only to that sector.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: They were established within the state security sector, and the public security sector had no authority over it. There was only one special operations unit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it was headed by the person whose name is shown in this schematic, Milorad Lukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: On this chart before you we see that there's a line between the special operations unit and the MUP staff for Kosovo. Was there any relationship, and if so what was it, between the special operations unit and the MUP staff of Kosovo which was headed by General Lukic was part of -- or JV, that is, public security department?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Sorry, are you asking me about special anti-terrorist units or about the special operations unit?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The special operations unit, the JSO. What was the relationship, if any, between them and the MUP staff of Kosovo? The MUP staff of Kosovo --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: I said already that the MUP staff for Kosovo had no authority over the JSO.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Coordination, joint meetings, analysing the security situation, consultations about particular assignments, all that existed; but the MUP staff did not have the authority to use -- to make the decision to use the JSO for special operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, what was the relationship and the hierarchy between the PJPs and the public security department headquarters in Belgrade? Or may I just rephrase the question. What was the relationship and the hierarchy of command between the PJPs in Kosovo and the public security department in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Well, the public security sector of the MUP of Serbia was the only one who could take decisions to use, to employ the PJPs in Kosovo and Metohija. While the commander of those units was in the hands of unit commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could move on. Can you tell us briefly about the number, the total number of police personnel in Kosovo between 1998 up to the NATO intervention in March 1999, and tell us if it fluctuated and why?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Well, in July 1998, anti-terrorist operations took place in Kosova and Metohija. At that time in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, there were 14.570 policemen. These operations lasted from the 25th of July until end September, 1998. With the signing of the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement, there was a reduction in the number of police personnel in Kosovo and Metohija. The number was reduced by 4.500. To be more precise, after the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement was signed, 10.021 policemen remained in Kosova-Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When was this agreement signed, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: It was signed in October of 1998, and in October this reduction took place. It was in the second half of the month of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And did the number of 10.000 plus policemen as of October 1998 remain the same going into 1999 or was there any -- or were there any changes?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Well, later in early 1999, or more precisely in March of 1999, there were some changes because we were threatened to -- we had immediate threat of war. And once the state of war was officially proclaimed, there was a change and the number was increased.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you describe further about when, if you can recall a date, did the mobilisation to increase the numbers begin, and what were the numbers eventually after the policemen were mobilised?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: The mobilisation, as a strategic act, encompasses two periods: the preparation of mobilisation and the execution of mobilisation. The preparation started earlier, it started in early 1999, or more precisely, in February of 1999. And the execution of the mobilisation started in March of 1999, that is, at a meeting held in the MUP headquarters in Pristina held on the 17th of March, 1999, General Lukic stated that all the Secretariats should prepare and undertake all the necessary measures to go forward with mobilisation of the members of the reserve police forces, so that the ratio between active policemen and reserve policemen should be one to one. More specifically, for SUP in Kosovska Mitrovica, this meant the following: In SUP Kosovska Mitrovica at the time we had 665 police officers, and we had to mobilise additional 665 reserve policemen in order to achieve this ratio of 1 to 1. Furthermore, he said that given that the negotiations at Rambouillet were very difficult, it could be realistically expected that we could have an act of aggression. At the very first sign that there will be an aggression, or the very first sign will be the withdrawal of the verifying mission from Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, we'll discuss that further later. For the time being, can we just see if we can establish figures. About how many policemen or what was the number of policemen approximately in Kosovo after mobilisation in March 1999?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Well, the number was the same as in 1998, and this is 14.571.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if you could tell us more precisely, I think you can, about your SUP in March after the mobilisation. How many policemen were there in total after mobilisation was completed?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: At Kosovska Mitrovica SUP there were regular police forces, then PJPs that were sent to Kosovska Mitrovica SUP, the 35th [Realtime transcript read in error, "55th"] and the 85th detachment, and also we had reserve police units that were trained in June of 1998 to be able to defend settlements, inhabited settlements. So each inhabited settlement in the territory of Kosova, which also means in the territory of SUP of Kosovska Mitrovica, had a Serb police unit. The regular police units of the SUP of Kosovska Mitrovica and members of PJPs, there were in total 1.990; and in reserve police units, we had a total of 6.034. So in total 8.033. This was the number of armed police officers in the territory of SUP Kosovska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before I proceed, Your Honours, just to point out that at line 7 of this page, I think the witness said the 35th and the 85th detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We are going to get to the reserve police units later, these were 6.000 plus men, I think you said. But just explain briefly for us what was the distinction between a reserve policeman and a member of a reserve police unit?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Reserve policemen could be reserves to the regular police units or reserves to the reserve police units. Reserve police units had a lower degree of training, lower degree of equipment, and weapons in comparison to the regular police units. These regular police units were subordinated to the Secretariats, so they were not tasked to defend inhabited settlements as were the reserve police units. The reserve police units did not even have an entire uniform, they just had parts of uniforms, for example, hats, possibly shirts or belts and so on. Reserve policemen on the other hand had the entire uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And when you say that the reserve police units were engaged to defend settlements, what do you mean by settlements?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: When I say inhabited settlements, I'm talking about various settlements within the territory of a municipality, so it's a village or a local commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could look at 0224 quickly, please. 01224, I believe. And go to page 2 in both, please. We are on the wrong page. Could I just find it. Could we go to page 2, page 3 in the English. I apologise for this, Your Honour, I had the number in the binder but apparently the document was taken out of the binder. Your Honours, having regard to the time, I think I could move on and I could get back to this tomorrow when I can find the -- find my copy of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'd like you to briefly describe for us what the security situation in Kosovo was in 1998. You told us about anti-terrorist operations that took place from July to September or October 1998. Were there any actions in your area, anti-terrorist actions in your area before that time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: Well, when I spoke, I said that the anti-terrorist operations started on July the 25th, 1998, and they lasted until the end of September of that year. The security situation in Kosovo was very difficult and very complicated. The terrorism was expanding. We had very many terrorist attacks against members of the police forces, but also against members of the army, Serbians, or loyal Albanians in Kosovo. There were quite a few persons killed, injured; Albanians, Serbs, or soldiers alike. And because of this, we decided to carry out anti-terrorist operations. Besides this, a number of companies and even a number of settlements were taken over by the terrorists. More specifically, in the territory of Kosovska Mitrovica SUP at the Trepca oil and steel factory which had one of its companies -- one of its plants in the village of Bare in Bajgora and which produced the equipment for [microphone not activated]. This particular plant was taken over by the terrorists, so the director of the company had no more control over his plant. In that particular factory, the terrorists started to produce uniforms for their members. In the settlement of Malisevo in Kosovo also fell to terrorists, and due to this very grave situation, because the movement was also very difficult, it was impossible to move at night in Kosovo at the time. All the communications were blocked. So it was decided at the staff to carry out anti-terrorist operations. However, it wasn't the staff's decision to carry out these operations, but rather this was the decision of the headquarters at the highest possible level with the so-called joined headquarters. When you asked me whether there were any anti-terrorist operations before July of 1998 in the territory of Kosovska Mitrovica SUP, I would like to point out that we did carry out an action whereby we wanted to catch a terrorist group and destroy the terrorist group, the so-called Drenica group in the settlement Donji Prekaz in the municipality of Srbica. This action was taken in the period between the 5th and 7th of March in three of the hamlets.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In this action, can you tell us where was -- if you know, where was this action conceived, planned, and who commanded the action?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: At that time, at the level of the Ministry of Interior, an intersectorial command was established --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Intersectorial staff was established.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And within that staff there were members of the public security sector and of the state security sector. The head of that joint staff was head of the state security sector and his deputy was chief of the public security sector. The planning and organisation of this particular action was the responsibility of this joint staff. And the units in the field were commanded by the commanders of these units. In this particular operation, the units of the Ministry of the Interior which took part in the operations, so besides the units of the Ministry of Interior also special anti-terrorist units of the state security sector participated in the operation. So we had the unit for special operations from the public security sector and special anti-terrorist units of the state security sector. The commanders of these units and a person from the Ministry of the Interior that was in charge of all the special anti-terrorist units were in the field, and also a person from the staff of the Pristina MUP and also deputy commander of the Pristina SUP staff were in the field and they took direct command over the units that participated in this particular operation. The decision on participation of these units in the operation was taken by this intersectorial staff. So most probably the intersectorial staff when making this decision also informed the highest level of the state authorities. This is my assumption because otherwise such an action could not have been planned nor organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who was chief of the RDB, the state security at that time, March of 1998?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN PNISHI
utterances.text: The chief of the state security sector at the time was Mr. Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, we've run over time, is that a convenient moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, it will be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We must adjourn now for the day and resume tomorrow morning at 9.00. So an officer of the court will give you more precise instructions, but we will continue your evidence in the morning at 9.00. Thank you.
